name: Sivanandeswarar Temple, Tirukkandalam
deity: Shiva as Sivanandeswarar (Tirukkalleeswarar), with the goddess Anandavalli
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Thondai country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with medieval and later additions
dynasty: Medieval Tamil patrons (Pallava and later Chola era)
summary: Sivanandeswarar at Tirukkandalam is the Tirukkallil of the Tevaram, a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Thondai country where the name is read from the kalli shrubs that once surrounded the Lord, and where tradition recalls both the sage Bhrigu's worship and Sambandar's visit.

sections.history: Tirukkandalam lies in the Thondai country north-west of Chennai, among the oldest living Shiva shrines of the region. In the Tevaram hymns the town is called Tirukkallil, and it is counted among the Thondai Nadu temples sung by the saints, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, praised by the child-saint Tirugnana Sambandar. The name Tirukkallil is read from the kalli, the thorny spurge that once grew thick about the place, for the Lord is said to have stood amid the kalli groves; over time the settlement came to be called Tirukkandalam. Raised and enlarged in stone by the patrons of the medieval Tamil country, the temple has been kept in continuous worship, a quiet village sanctuary that carries the memory of the hymns sung here many centuries ago.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a five-tiered rajagopuram that rises over the village. Just outside the gateway lies the temple tank, the Nandi Theertham, which tradition says was formed by Nandi himself, and the flagstaff, the balipeetam, and the seated Nandi are ranged in a single line with the eastern doorway. Within the enclosure the sanctum holds the Shiva linga, honoured as a swayambhu, self-manifest, facing east. The shrine of the goddess Anandavalli and the shrine of Murugan stand to the side of the sanctum and both face east as well, so that Lord, Goddess, and the child Murugan are aligned in the manner of the Somaskanda, an arrangement devotees hold to be the temple's distinctive feature.
sections.legends: Two stories gather at Tirukkallil. In the first, the sage Bhrigu is said to have worshipped here with a thousand kalli flowers, and Shiva, pleased, revealed himself to the rishi as Dakshinamurthy, the silent teacher facing south. In the second, the saint Sambandar came to the town and set down the articles of his worship on the riverbank before going to bathe; when he returned they were nowhere to be found. Searching, he came at last upon them placed beside the swayambhu linga within the temple, and understood that the Lord had drawn his offerings there to bring the saint himself to the shrine. Moved, Sambandar sang a decad in praise of Sivanandeswarar, and by that hymn the town took its place among the sung shrines of the Tevaram.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the festivals of the Shaiva year with devotion. Tirukarthikai in Karthikai (November–December) and the Karthigai Deepam are observed with lamps, Maha Shivaratri in Masi (February–March) is kept with night-long worship, and Skanda Sashti in Aippasi honours Murugan in his east-facing shrine. Margazhi Tiruvadhirai and the Aippasi full-moon Annabhishekam are also marked, along with Vinayaka Chaturthi and Navaratri. The monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Tirukkandalam rewards a quiet, unhurried visit. Enter beneath the five-tiered eastern gopuram, pause at the Nandi Theertham tank before the gateway, and come through the line of flagstaff and Nandi to the sanctum of Sivanandeswarar and his self-manifest linga. Turn then to the goddess Anandavalli and to Murugan in their east-facing shrines, where the Somaskanda alignment can be felt. Away from the main Chennai roads, the temple keeps the stillness of a village sanctuary, and devotees who come for the hymns of Sambandar find the place little changed in spirit from the days the saints passed through.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirukkandalam lies about 40 km north-west of Chennai and roughly 10 km from Periyapalayam, near Kannigaipper in Tiruvallur district. Buses on route 58-D from Chennai's Koyambedu market towards Vengal pass through the village with a stop near the temple. The nearest large towns are Tiruvallur and Periyapalayam, with Chennai the nearest airport and major railhead.
